aiSummary: Speckled trout and redfish are the story on Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with solid trout numbers on the grass flats and bull reds showing up in recent reports — fish early, as 87°F water is pushing the bite hard toward dawn and well before midday heat sets in. A new moon spring tide is driving stronger-than-usual tidal movement today, with high tide just after sunrise and low tide in the late afternoon, giving anglers a productive moving-water window through mid-morning. A 21% storm chance kicks in after 1 PM, so plan to be off the open water by early afternoon and lean toward protected bayous if you're staying out late.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Its pilings hold trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Keep in mind this is open, exposed water — it's typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind builds or weather rolls in.
bridge.todaysCall: The new moon spring tide means stronger-than-normal current through this funnel, and the outgoing tide running toward the 4:55 PM low should push bait hard through the pilings all afternoon — but the post-1 PM storm window makes a long afternoon session risky here on open water. Hit the bridge early: high tide was at 6:04 AM right at sunrise, so the tide will be dropping and moving through the pilings during the prime morning window. WSW winds at 5–10 mph are light enough to keep chop manageable for now, but conditions can deteriorate fast at this exposed spot. Focus on the lee-side pilings with live or cut bait for trout and drum, and plan to clear out well before 1 PM.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the creek mouth. The oyster bars at the mouth are the prime target, and tree cover keeps interior water a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish conditions and can hold bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: Tree cover and protected geometry make Alaqua a smart choice on a day with afternoon storm risk — you can fish later here than you could on open water and still have an exit plan. The spring tide's stronger tidal pull will be moving water through those oyster bars all morning off the 6:04 AM high, concentrating baitfish and trout right at the creek mouth. With water at 87°F across the open bay, the slightly cooler interior of Alaqua gives redfish and trout a thermal refuge — work the shaded banks and oyster edges during the outgoing tide. Slightly stained water favors noisier or darker lures like a dark-colored soft plastic or gold spinnerbait to help fish locate the bait.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to mean less-educated fish and more willing biters. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for reds in under two feet of water. Pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer, and the bayou is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds.
basin.todaysCall: Lower pressure here is a genuine advantage on a summer weekday — if trout and reds are stacked on interior flats elsewhere, they're stacked here too with fewer boats competing. Work the interior grass flats for reds early while water clarity is at its best and before midday heat stresses fish in the shallows; slightly stained water calls for slower presentations and lures with some rattle or vibration. The outgoing tide off this morning's high will push baitfish toward the mouth through mid-morning — a good window to intercept trout there as well. Be mindful that Basin offers less weather protection than LaGrange; if the sky starts building before 1 PM, have an exit plan ready.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer on this side of the bay, built around legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold reds year-round. Deep holes inside harbor black drum and sheepshead, and the bayou offers the most protected water in this area — the go-to refuge when weather builds anywhere on the bay.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the strongest all-around call for today: the spring tide will be pushing hard off this morning's high tide, running water across those oyster bars right during the prime early-morning bite window. Recent reports from the past week or two show speckled trout as the standout bay species across the grass flats, and LaGrange's oyster-bar and flat setup fits that pattern precisely — fish topwaters or suspending twitch baits early before switching to soft plastics as the sun climbs. With a 21% storm chance after 1 PM and LaGrange being the most protected spot on this dashboard, you can reasonably fish later here than almost anywhere else while still having shelter if weather builds. Slightly stained water means fish are relying more on lateral line — slow down your retrieve and give trout time to find the bait.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates reds and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water where bass and small reds can be found. Its compact, protected character makes it one of the safest options when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is an excellent bail-out option if storm cells fire earlier than the 1 PM forecast window — it's short, protected, and close to the ramp. This morning's outgoing tide is your primary window: water moving off the 6:04 AM high will push baitfish out of the creek and concentrate predators at the bends, grass edges, and especially the mouth where flounder set up to ambush. WSW winds at 5–10 mph won't affect this creek much given its orientation and tree cover, so conditions should stay fishable all morning. Work soft plastics or paddle-tails slowly along the bottom at the mouth for flounder, then move up into the bends for reds and trout on the falling water.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay, with summer mornings particularly strong as trout stack on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, and the bayou sees regular guide pressure but produces reliably. It sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous, so factor in run time when planning your trip.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown's grass flats in two to four feet are exactly the habitat where bay-wide reports have been finding speckled trout recently — this is one of the best setups on the dashboard for today's pattern if you're willing to make the run. Leave the dock at or before first light to capitalize on the outgoing tide off the 6:04 AM high and to beat both the heat and any early-developing convection; by mid-morning the 93°F air and 87°F water will push fish off the shallowest flats. Spanish mackerel at the mouth are a bonus target during the moving-tide morning window — have a fast-moving spoon or small jig ready near the bayou entrance. Factor the longer run time into your storm-window math: with cells possible after 1 PM, you want to start your return before noon.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport, and its direct connection to that top-producing system means LaGrange's oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water. There is far less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself, so treat it as a secondary option rather than a proven standalone destination. Its small, interior character makes it a likely calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: If you're already running LaGrange and find it pressured or picked over, Mallet Bayou is a logical and low-effort extension — same tidal push, same species, with almost certainly fewer boats. The spring tide off this morning's high will be moving water through this small tributary too, which can concentrate baitfish and feeding reds in the tighter bends and edges. Slightly stained water actually helps here, giving reds confidence to root along the shallower interior without spooking as easily. Manage expectations on documented bite history, but the habitat and LaGrange connection make it worth a look as a bonus stop.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination, not a quick local trip. It shares the same protected bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, and sees lighter pressure simply due to its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack is the main calculus today: with a 21% storm chance after 1 PM, you need to be confident in an early start and a firm turnaround time before that window opens. If you commit to a dawn departure, the spring tide off the 6:04 AM high will be moving water across Mack's oyster bars right during the first fishable light — a strong setup for trout and reds on the outgoing. Light pressure on this side of the bay is a real edge in summer when other spots see guide traffic early. Plan a Mack-Hewett-Buck circuit to maximize the run time investment, fish hard until 11 AM, and start heading back well before storm risk rises.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou as part of the same long-run trip from the 331 Bridge. Its habitat mirrors its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth with deeper interior holes further in — and it receives light pressure due to its distance from the main ramps.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as part of the Mack-Hewett-Buck circuit given the long run involved — same trip, same tides, same species, just working east along the barrier-island shoreline. The outgoing tide off the 6:04 AM high will be running through Hewett's mouth structure during the early-morning window, which is where you want to focus first with trout and redfish likely holding on the oyster bars. Slightly stained water means fish are less likely to spook on approach in the shallower interior, which is an advantage for working soft plastics tight to the grass edges. Mirror the same storm-window discipline as Mack — be moving back toward the 331 Bridge well before 1 PM.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about consistent fishing there. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination worth the long run on its own.
buck.todaysCall: Buck makes sense only as the third stop on a Mack-Hewett-Buck run — the run time alone rules it out as a solo destination, especially on a day with afternoon storm risk. If you've worked Mack and Hewett through the morning outgoing tide and still have time before your 1 PM turnaround, swing through Buck's mouth to probe the oyster and grass structure for any reds or trout that didn't commit earlier. Keep expectations measured given limited fishing documentation here, but the habitat connection to its neighbors means the same early-morning moving-tide approach applies. Don't linger — your priority is being well clear of open water on the long run back before storm cells can develop.
